name: Victor Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Victor, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the marketing specialist at a regional brewery. We make about a dozen beers that go to pubs, shops and a few supermarkets. A normal day is writing labels and social posts, planning events like beer festivals and brewery tours, and working with our sales team on what pubs need. I love the events; I'm less keen on the endless social media posts, which feel like shouting into a well.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then, mostly to get ideas for a beer name or a post. I check everything myself. I live with my girlfriend Lucia, who's a dental nurse, and I've got about four months of costs saved. On Sundays I play guitar in the church band, which keeps me grounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it doesn't change much. Sounds believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for some things, but people still drink beer with people. I'd probably post something like that. At work I'd keep using it for name ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel secure. Pub landlords don't buy our beer because of a clever slogan; they buy because I turned up at the beer festival and shook their hand. The brewery's doing fine, and they like that I know the pubs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and keep saving a bit each month. I'd push to do more events, because that's where I'm useful. Lucia and I might start looking at houses in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty happy, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the brewery's situation, honestly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Beer sales go up and down with the weather, but they've been around thirty years. The owner, Frank, is old-fashioned, and that helps here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia's hours at the dental practice got cut a bit this year. It's fine, but it makes me keep an eye on the money.

I'd keep using it for **name ideas** at work.
think: I privately feel **secure** at a steady brewery that values my pub contacts.
Pub landlords buy because of **handshakes**, not slogans.
do: Push to run more **events** and festivals.
Start looking at **houses** with Lucia in a year or two.

steps.text: Keep running the brewery's festival and tour calendar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a lot of my desk work, right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and people have always had to adapt. I'd say the brewery should keep people who know the customers. I wouldn't go on about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried the labels and posts go to software. The software can write the label for our harvest ale, but it can't sit in a pub on a Tuesday night and convince a landlord to give us a tap. I'd want to move toward that side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more for the routine posts so I have time for pub visits. I'd ask Frank about moving into trade sales. I'd keep saving and put off house hunting a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared yet, but I'd be thinking about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Trade sales pays differently. Would that work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's partly commission, so it's riskier. But if I'm good at it, it could pay more. I'd have to be confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the brewery would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our designer, Kasia. She does labels and posters, and that's exactly what these tools are getting good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after each other, families and churches especially. I'd say government shouldn't just hand out money but should help people learn trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect my marketing job to go fast. Two years is no time at all, so I'd ask the head brewer to take me on as an apprentice before the brewery even has a plan. Brewing is hands-on, so it should last a few years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about an apprenticeship in the brewhouse straight away. I'd cut spending and stop house hunting. Lucia and I might move in with my parents for a year to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come three years later. What then for brewing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe the big breweries go robot first and small ones last longer. I'd hope so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Lucia feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but she'd back me. Her dental work is hands-on too, so we'd both have a few years.

think: I privately expect my marketing job to **go fast**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That gives some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had a warning, so let's plan. I'd tell younger people to look at trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the marketing desk job goes by 2031. With five years I'd move from writing about beer to selling it face to face, because pub landlords trust a person they've had a pint with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move into trade sales and spend more time in pubs. I'd keep saving. I'd also learn a bit of brewing on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why both sales and brewing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know which lasts longer. Sales needs people until AI can talk like one; brewing needs hands until robots arrive. Two options feels safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in year three, if sales goes well. I'd want to be sure first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a fair bit of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people to learn new trades properly. I'd say that's how it should be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. Ten years is enough time to learn brewing properly, and I'd rather make the beer than write about it when the computers take the writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep my job and use the AI tools where they help. I'd start a part-time brewing course. Lucia and I would buy a house in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive around 2039 here. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I'd be 40, with a trade and maybe a family. I'd cross that bridge then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia and I want them in a few years. Ten years makes that feel safe enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Every generation in my family has had to change trades once, and I'd rather choose my change than wait for someone to choose it for me. What would help is apprenticeships for adults and employers being encouraged to train their own people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith and family. They're what I'd lean on, more than any government scheme.

headlineQuote: Every generation in my family has had to change trades once, and I'd rather choose my change than wait for someone to choose it for me.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old marketer** at a regional brewery, living with Lucia, a dental nurse.
He uses AI **now and then** and values pub relationships most.
He believes in **family, faith and trades**, not handouts.
He moves from calm to **alarmed** at two years, easing with more time.
His fallback is **trade sales** or a brewing apprenticeship.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because there'd be **no time** to choose his own change.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **adult apprenticeships** and employers training their own people.
